However, 2D6 (and CYP enzymes in general) may play a minor role in the in vivo metabolic pathway and clearance based on the lack of NADPH-dependent loss of MEAI observed in the HLM fraction.

 

81

 

 

PK Drug Interaction Studies

 

Four in vitro drug interaction studies were conducted to characterize the effects of MEAI as an inhibitor or a substrate on different human transporters, as summarized below. These studies are based on the “In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies — Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions Guidance for Industry” (January 2020 Clinical Pharmacology). Phenotyping in renal and hepatic transporters (OATP1B1/3 & OAT1/3 OCT1/2 & MATE1/MATE2-K) was conducted because of the molecular structure of MEAI (small and polar) and because of possible hepatically impaired target population, respectively.

 

●An in-vitro drug interaction study was conducted to determine the potential of MEAI to inhibit the activity of P glycoprotein (P-gp) transporter in Caco-2 cells. Caco-2 cells were seeded in 96-wells and cultured for 24 days. The seeded cells were incubated with either vehicle control or increasing doses (ranging between 0.05 to 100 µM) of MEAI. After 2 hours incubation, the bi-directional permeability and efflux ratios of digoxin (10 µM), a known P-gp substrate were determined using LC-MS/MS. The IC50 was calculated by %P-gp activity values. Under the conditions tested, the %P-gp activity values of Caco-2 cells treated with MEAI were no less than 76.3, therefore, the IC50 value of MEAI on P-gp was greater than 100 µM, indicating that MEAI is not an inhibitor of the P-gp transporter.

 

●An additional in-vitro drug interaction study was conducted to determine the bidirectional permeability and the P-gp (P glycoprotein) substrate potential of MEAI in Caco-2 cells. Caco-2 cells were seeded on 96-well and cultured for 24 days. The seeded cells were incubated with MEAI at 2.0, 10,0 and 100 µM with or without potent P-gp inhibitors, 30.0 µM verapamil and 1.00 µM zosuquidar. Samples were taken at 0 and after 2 hours incubation and analyzed by LC MS/MS. Results indicate that under the conditions tested, MEAI demonstrated high permeability across the Caco-2 cell monolayer and was a poor or non-P gp substrate.

 

●A third in-vitro drug interaction study was conducted to determine the potential of MEAI to inhibit the activities of different renal and hepatic transporters (OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, MATE1, and MATE2-K). HEK-293 cells expressing the different transporters were incubated with the relevant substrates in the absence and presence of different doses of MEAI (ranging between 0.05 and 100 μM). MEAI inhibited OCT1 and OCT2 with the IC50 values of 1.67 and 22.3 µM, respectively. HEK293- cells expressing OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, MATE1, and MATE2-K transporters had activity expressed as % of Vehicle Control (VC) values of no less than 98.2, 81.8, 95.0, 97.8, 80.3, and 58.4, respective to each transporter. Therefore, the IC50 values of MEAI on OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, MATE1, and MATE2-K were greater than 100 μM, indicating MEAI had no effect on the activity of these transporters. Overall, except for OCT1 and OCT2 where a mild inhibition was found, MEAI had no effect on transporters activity.

 

●A fourth in-vitro drug interaction study was conducted to determine whether MEAI is a potential substrate to different renal and hepatic transporters (OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, MATE1, and MATE2-K). HEK-293 cells expressing the different transporters and HEK293-mock cells were incubated with MEAI in the presence and absence of an inhibitor for each of the above-mentioned transporters. The concentrations of MEAI in the cell lysate samples were quantitatively determined by LC-MS/MS after protein precipitation, and the uptake fold (the ratio of transport activity between the transporter transfected cells and HEK293-MOCK cells) and Rs/Ri (the ratio of transport activity in the transporter transfected cells without and with the inhibitor) values of the test compound were calculated. For each transporter, three concentrations of MEAI were tested: 1.00, 10.0, and 100 µM. Results show that the Rs/Ri values were less than 2 in all transporters tested, except for OCT1 and OCT2. Furthermore, the increase in uptake fold for all transporters tested was less than 2-fold. Overall, these results indicated that MEAI is not a substrate for the transporters test.

 

In conclusion, these drug interaction studies indicated that under the conditions tested MEAI has no effect as an inhibitor or a substrate on different human transporters, except for OCT1 and OCT2 transporters, for which a mild effect was observed.

 

Toxicological studies

 

The toxicological effects of MEAI were studies in a variety of animals models in two species (mainly rats and dogs) and included both single and repeat dose toxicity studies, genotoxicity, and special toxicity studies. These are summarized below.

 

82

 

 

10-Days Repeat Dose Rage Finding Toxicity Study of MEAI in Rats

 

An in vivo study was conducted in rats to determine the potential toxicity of MEAI when administered once daily by oral administration for 10 days. In addition, the toxicokinetic (TK) of MEAI were determined. For this purpose, 82 rats (41/sex) were randomly assigned to 4 groups, 5 rats/sex/group for the main study animals, and 3 animals/sex in the control TK group and 6 animals/sex/group in test article TK groups. Animals in the test article treated groups were administered with MEAI by oral gavage once daily at 20, 40, or 80 mg/kg/day for up to 10 days. Animals in the control group were dosed once daily with the vehicle only for 10 days. Animals were monitored for viability (morbidity/mortality), clinical observations, body weight, food consumption, clinical pathology (hematology, serum chemistry, coagulation), gross (necropsy) evaluation, organ weight, histopathological evaluation (select tissues in the control and high-dose groups) and toxicokinetic. After single (Day 1) or repeated (Day 10) oral administration of MEAI to male and female rats, Tmax MEAI generally occurred between 2.0 and 4.0 hours post dose. T1/2 values MEAI ranged from 2.03 and 4.66 hours. No marked sex difference in systemic exposure (AUC0-24h and/or Cmax) was observed at any dose level. Overall, as the dosage increased from 20 to 80 mg/kg/day, the systemic exposure (AUC0-24h and Cmax) increased in an approximately dose proportional manner in both sexes on Day 1 and Day 10. No marked drug accumulation and no differences in systemic exposure with repeated dosing were observed at any dose level. From the safety point of view, test article-related changes in clinical signs were noted in male and female animals at all dose levels but were only adverse at 80 mg/kg/day. Additional findings at 80 mg/kg/day were nasal discharge, skin discolored, activity decreased, cold to touch, coat soiled, hunched posture, atonia and/or piloerection. Minor changes at 20 and 40 mg/kg/day included salivation, hypersensitive to touch, and/or material around mouth were noted. One female dosed at 80 mg/kg/day was found dead on Day 1 without any gross lesions. This animal exhibited salivation, atonia and piloerection prior to death and histopathology revealed microscopic changes in the adrenal glands (mild cortical congestion/hemorrhage), mandibular and mesenteric lymph nodes (minimal lymphocytic necrosis/decreased cellularity), and vagina (mucosal mucification). These changes were most likely secondary to overt stress but were not sufficient to contribute to the animal’s death directly. Thus, the cause of death could not be determined based on anatomic pathology evaluations. All animals gained weight over the 10-day treatment period, but this was significantly decreased in the high-dose males at each interval; mean body weight was also decreased in the 80 mg/kg/day males. No adverse test article-related changes on body weight and weight gain were noted at 20 and 40 mg/kg/day. A dose-related, statistically significant decrease in food consumption was observed at all doses. There were no test article-related changes in hematology and coagulation parameters at any dose level. At ≥20 mg/kg/day, significant dose dependent increases in Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) were noted in treated animals when compared with the control group. Test article-related organ weight changes were present in the adrenal glands, spleen, and thymus.

 

These alterations are shown in Mean absolute and relative (to brain or bodyweight) splenic weights were decreased for males at ≥40 mg/kg/day and females at ≥ 20 mg/kg/day, correlating microscopically with atrophy for animals at 80 mg/kg/day. There were no test article-related macroscopic changes in any treatment groups. Test article-related microscopic changes occurred in the spleen. Minimal, diffuse atrophy occurred in the spleen of both sexes at 80 mg/kg/day. This change was characterized by a decrease in the size of the white and red pulps proportionally, resulting in a reduction in the overall size of the spleen. The microscopic finding of multifocal mononuclear infiltration with few hepatocellular necrosis around the central vein was noted in both sexes at the control and high dose groups. Although the severity of this change was slightly increased for animals in the high dose group, it was a common background finding consistent with the age and strain of this species. Thus, its relationship to the test article was unclear. In conclusion, MEAI caused some toxicity in SD rats dosed once daily for 10 days at 80 mg/kg/day as seen by mortality, adverse clinical signs, decreases in weight gain and food consumption, alterations in hematology and clinical chemistry parameters, and splenic atrophy. Doses of 20 and 40 mg/kg/day were generally well tolerated and did not markedly impact the overall health of the rats. Therefore, under the conditions of the study, the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) was 40 mg/kg/day. The corresponding Day 10 AUC0-24h and Cmax values MEAI were 17500 ng●hr/mL and 2380 ng/mL for males, and 26700 ng●hr/mL and 4210 ng/mL for females, respectively.

 

A Single Escalating Dose Followed by a 10-Days Repeat Dose Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study of MEAI in Beagle Dogs

 

An in vivo 10-days repeat dose study was also conducted in beagle dogs. In this study the potential toxicity of MEAI was evaluated in 2 phases. In Phase A (dose escalating phase), MEAI was administered in a single dose escalating manner (once daily or twice daily [BID] approximately 8 hours apart) until the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was reached. In Phase B (repeat dose phase), MEAI was administrated once daily for 10 consecutive days. In addition, the toxicokinetics (TK) of MEAI were determined in Phase B.

 

83

 

 

In Phase A, 4 dogs (2/sex) were randomly assigned to 2 groups of 1/sex and administered MEAI by oral gavage at a single dose of 15, 20, 30, 40 and 45 mg/kg for the males and 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and 40 mg/kg for the females. The vehicle was sterile water. Animals were monitored for viability (morbidity/mortality), clinical observations, body weight and food consumption. Generally minor, transient clinical signs were noted at 15 to 40/35 mg/kg (male/female) with more pronounced and adverse signs at 45/40 mg/kg (male/female). The main clinical observations were salivation, hypersensitivity to touch and tremors. At the high-dose, other findings included increased respiratory rate in the female and prostration. The signs recovered by the next day. One male at the high dose was found dead at about 1 hour after dosing. Prior to being found dead, the animal had shown signs of being hypersensitive to touch, salivation, tremors, and prostration. The macroscopic examination showed swelling in the lungs (likely to be edema), foamy red fluid from the trachea, multifocal white discoloration (raised) in the mucosa of the cecum and enlarged liver. These macroscopic changes were not observed at the scheduled termination of the Phase B dogs, but the male had the highest dose administered in this study, 45 mg/kg. The relationship with test article was uncertain, but it could not be ruled out. Transient decreases were reported in body weight (20 and 30 mg/kg in males and 15 to 30 mg/kg in females) and food consumption (15 to 40 mg/kg in females), which resolved quickly. Overall MEAI, when administered by oral gavage once to beagle dogs at doses up to 45 mg/kg in males and 40 mg/kg in females, resulted in mortality in a male dog at 45 mg/kg as well as decreases in body weight and food consumption at 45/40 mg/kg (male/female). Therefore, under the conditions of this phase of the study, the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was 40 mg/kg for both males and females. Based on the clinical signs, the high dose of 35 mg/kg/day was proposed for the females and of 40 mg/kg/day for the males in Phase B of the study.

 

In Phase B of the study, a total of 16 dogs (8/sex) were randomly assigned to 4 groups of 2/sex/group and administered MEAI by oral gavage at the doses of 0 (Sterile water), 10, 20, and 40/35 (males/females) mg/kg/day once daily for 10 days. The animals were monitored for viability (morbidity/mortality), clinical observations, body weight, food consumption, clinical pathology (hematology, serum chemistry, coagulation), and toxicokinetics. Animals were euthanized at the end of the study for gross pathology evaluation, organ weight and histopathological evaluation. After once daily oral administration of MEAI at 10, 20, and 40/35 mg/kg/day to dogs for 10 days, the toxicokinetic data revealed Tmax values between 0.5 and 8.0 hours post dose. No marked sex difference in systemic exposure was observed at 10 and 20 mg/kg/day. The systemic exposure increased in an approximately dose proportional manner in males and a slightly less than dose proportional manner in females on Days 1 and 10 as the dosage increased from 10 to 35 mg/kg/day in females and from 10 to 40 mg/kg/day in males. No marked drug accumulation or differences in systemic exposure were observed at any dose level with repeated dosing. There were no moribund or found dead animals during this phase of the study. There were no test article-related changes in clinical pathology, organ weights, gross pathology and microscopic pathology at any dose. As occurred in Phase A, the main clinical signs included salivation, hypersensitivity to touch, and tremors. There were no findings at 10 mg/kg/day. At 20 mg/kg/day, salivation (both sexes) and hypersensitivity to touch and tremors (female) occurred. The most pronounced and persistent clinical signs were reported at the high dose (40/35 mg/kg/day [male/female]) and included ocular discharge, salivation, hypersensitivity to touch, tremors, and convulsions (Day 7 only for the male and Day 2 only for the female). On the Day 10, test article-related body weight decreases were noted at 40 mg/kg/day in the males, and at 10, 20, and 35 mg/kg/day for the females. These body weight decreases correlated with the observed food consumption decreases. The changes at 20 mg/kg/day for the females and 40/35 for males and females were toxicologically meaningful. In conclusion, administration of MEAI to beagle dogs once daily for 10 days by oral gavage at dosages of 10, 20 and 40/35 mg/kg/day did not result in any test article -related mortality. The low- and mid-doses resulted in minor toxicity. In addition, weight loss over the 10-day treatment period and transient decreases in food consumption were noted in the females at 20 mg/kg/day. In comparison, the high-dose produced tremors, convulsions, and significant and toxicologically meaningful decreases in body weight and food consumption. There were no test article-related effects on clinical pathology, gross pathology, organ weights or histopathology at any dose. Therefore, under the conditions of this phase of the study, the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) was considered to be 10 mg/kg/day in females and 20 mg/kg/day in males. The corresponding Day 10 AUC0-24h and Cmax values at the NOAEL were 32900 ng●hr/mL and 4590 ng/mL for females, and 48600 ng●hr/mL and 5450 ng/mL for males, respectively.

 

84

 

 

A 28-Days Repeat Dose Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study of MEAI in Rats with a 14-Day Recovery Period

 

An in vivo GLP study was conducted in rats to evaluate the potential toxicity of MEAI, when administered once daily by oral gavage to rats for up to 28 days and to assess the reversibility, persistence, or delayed occurrence of toxic effects following a 14 Day recovery period. In addition, the toxicokinetics (TK) of MEAI were determined.

 

For this purpose, 162 rats (81/sex) were randomly assigned to 4 groups of 15 animals/sex/group in the main study. These were daily treated with either vehicle (WFI) or MEAI at three different doses (20, 40 or 80 mg/kg) by oral gavage for 28 days. For TK evaluation, 3 animals/sex/group were assigned to receive vehicle and 6 animals/sex/group were treated with MEAI at the same conditions as in the main study. The last 5 surviving main study animals/sex/group from all groups were allocated for recovery and functional observations battery test.

 

Criteria for evaluation included viability (morbidity/mortality), clinical observations, body weight, food consumption, ophthalmologic examinations, functional observational battery, clinical pathology (hematology, serum chemistry, coagulation, urinalyses), macroscopic observations, organ weight, histopathological evaluation and toxicokinetics.

 

The toxicokinetic data collected revealed that Tmax values were generally observed between 1.0 and 2.0 hours post-dose. No marked sex differences in systemic exposure were observed at any dose level. The systemic exposure increased approximately dose proportionally in both sexes on Day 1 and Day 28 as the dosage increased from 20 to 80 mg/kg/day. Generally, no marked drug accumulation was observed at any dose level.

 

There were seven early deaths reported among five main study and two TK study animals given 80 mg/kg/day. Main study animals were found dead on Day 1 and Day 25, and TK animals were found dead on Day 2 and Day 3. Prior to being found dead, animals showed clinical signs such as slight to moderate salivation, tremors, unkempt, increased respiratory rate, ocular discharge, red material around nose, skin discolored, hypersensitive to touch, hunched posture, decreased activity, slight prepuce swelling, penis extended and/or soiled coat. No test article-related changes in body weights, body weight gains, food consumption, macroscopic or microscopic changes were observed for the five main study animals, and the cause of death was undetermined. No test article-related macroscopic changes were observed and no microscopic examination was performed for the two TK study animals, therefore, the cause of death was undetermined. All other animals survived to scheduled necropsy.

 

There were no test article-related changes in ophthalmology, hematology, coagulation, serum chemistry and urinalysis during this study. In addition, there were no test article-related macroscopic or microscopic findings following the dosing or recovery phases.

 

The primary finding in this study was test article-related clinical signs. These were noted at ≥ 20 mg/kg/day for both males and females in the dosing phase and included: coat soiled (abdomen, neck, head/dorsal, head); hunched posture; salivation; abnormal gait; activity decreased; hypersensitive to touch; tremors; skin discolored (ears, forefeet, forelimb, hindfeet, hindlimbs/bilateral, tail/distal, nose); prepuce swelling; unkempt; ocular discharge (eye/bilateral or left or right); increased respiratory rate; penis extended and/or material around (mouth, nose). The number of animals affected, and the frequency of signs observed increased with increasing dose and were mostly observed at the 80 mg/kg/day high dose level. Symptoms of coat soiled, hunched posture, salivation, hypersensitive to touch, skin discolored and ocular discharge appeared from the beginning of the dosing (or mid-dosing) period and lasted almost until the end of the dosing period. In the recovery phase, hunched posture and hypersensitive to touch persisted at ≥ 40 mg/kg/day for females for approximately 1 week. The rest of the symptoms observed during the dosing period recovered.

 

Test article-related and statistically significantly decreased body weight gains were noted at ≥ 20 mg/kg/day for males and persisted throughout the dosing period at 40 and 80 mg/kg/day whereas for females, this was only noted at 80 mg/kg/day on Day 7. Mean body weight decreased in males up to 15% decrease when compared to the concurrent controls, this decrease was dose dependent. and up to 4.86% in females at 80 mg/kg/day. The magnitude of the decrease in body weight gain increased as the dosing progressed for males at all dose groups. This decrease in group mean body weight and weight gain correlated with decreased mean food consumption during the dosing phase. In the recovery phase, weight gains were comparable to or greater than the control animals. However, the group male mean body weights still remained lower than the controls.

 

Significant reductions in food consumption were observed for animals from all treated groups; these generally were dose-dependent. For the males this persisted throughout the 28-day dosing period whereas for the females the effect was more transient with group mean food consumption for treated animals being comparable to the controls during the last two weeks of dosing. The decreased group mean food consumption correlated with decreased body weight gain. In the recovery phase, all animals showed significant and notable recovery, with food consumption for treated animals being higher than the controls.

 

85

 

 

Test article related central nervous function reversible changes, noted at ≥20 mg/kg/day, included increased resistance to removal from home cage, reduced rearing frequency, straub tail, salivation, increased body tone (firm), increased forelimb strength, wider hindlimb splay and/or decreased rectal temperature on Days 1 and 23 at 2 hours post-dose. These largely resolved by 24 hours on each of the dosing days. There were no findings at the recovery (Day 41) assessment.

 

Group mean terminal body weights were significantly lower than the control mean for males given 40 or 80 mg/kg/day. Spleen weights (absolute and relative to body and brain weight) were statistically significantly lower than the respective control means for animals given 80 mg/kg/day, with no correlating macroscopic or microscopic changes. Thyroid weights (absolute and relative to brain and body weight) were statistically significantly lower than the control means for females given 40 or 80 mg/kg/day. There were no correlating macroscopic or microscopic changes. No test article-related organs weight changes were noted following the recovery phase.

 

In conclusion, MEAI when administered by oral administration to Sprague Dawley rats once daily for up to 28 days followed by a 14-day recovery period at dosages of 20, 40 or 80 mg/kg/day resulted in adverse effects at 40 and 80 mg/kg/day. The primary finding was adverse clinical signs, which were noted at all doses, but were considered to be adverse at 40 mg/kg/day and above. Mortality occurred only at 80 mg/kg/day. Body weight and food consumption changes were also noted at the mid- and high-doses, but were most pronounced at the high-dose. Collectively, the changes at 20 mg/kg/day were not considered to be adverse and, therefore, under the conditions of this study, the NOAEL for MEAI was considered to be 20 mg/kg/day. The corresponding AUC0-24h and Cmax of MEAI following the last dose were 23200 h*ng/mL and 2970 ng/mL in males, and 30000 h*ng/mL and 3660 ng/mL in females, respectively.

 

A 28-Days Repeat Dose Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study of MEAI in Beagle Dogs with a 14-Day Recovery Period

 

An in vivo GLP study was conducted in beagle dogs in order to determine the potential toxicity of MEAI, when administered by oral dose to Beagle Dog for 28 Days and to assess the reversibility, persistence, or delayed occurrence of toxic effects following a 14 Day recovery period. In addition, the toxicokinetics (TK) of MEAI will be determined.

 

Forty-eight dogs (24 animals/sex) were randomly assigned to 4 groups of 6 animals/sex/group and given vehicle or MEAI formulated in vehicle at doses of 5, 15, or 30→25 mg/kg/day once daily for up to 28 days via oral gavage. Animals were randomly assigned to groups based on body weight. The last 2 dogs/sex/group from all groups were allocated for recovery and functional observation battery tests. Due to severe toxicity (death) in high dose group, the dose level was decreased from 30 to 25 mg/kg/day from Day 3 for males and Day 2 for females.

 

Criteria for evaluation included mortality, clinical signs, body weights, food consumption, ophthalmic examinations, safety pharmacology (electrocardiography, blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration examinations), clinical pathology (hematology, coagulation, serum chemistry, and urinalysis), toxicokinetics, organ weights, and macroscopic and microscopic examinations.

 

The toxicokinetic data collected revealed that the Tmax values were between 1.0 and 12.0 hours post-dose. Median T1/2 values ranged from 2.5 and 6.2 hours. No marked sex differences in systemic exposure were observed at any dose level. The systemic exposure increased dose proportionally in males and females on Days 1 and 28 as the dosage increased from 5 to 30 mg/kg/day (on Day 1) and from 5 to 25 mg/kg/day (on Day 28). No marked drug accumulation was observed at 5 and 15 mg/kg/day.

 

Test article-related mortality occurred at 30 mg/kg/day. One male and one female were found dead on study Day 1. Before being found dead, clinical observations of salivation, tremors, opisthotonus, high body temperature, convulsions were noted in both animals. Findings at necropsy included red discoloration of various organs due to congestion and peracute hemorrhage. The cause of death in both animals was attributed to peracute hemorrhage involving the heart and lungs.

 

86

 

 

There were no test article-related changes in ophthalmic examinations, coagulation, urinalysis, organ weights, macroscopic and microscopic evaluations in scheduled terminated animals. Test article-related clinical signs including abnormal vocalization, increased activity, ataxia, convulsions, opisthotonus, hypersensitive to touch noted in males and/or females at 30→25 mg/kg/day and tremors noted in both sexes at 15 mg/kg/day and 30→25 mg/kg/day at the beginning of dosing phase (Days 1-4). Isolated incidents of salivation, decreased activity, discolored skin, discharge ocular, vomitus and discolored conjunctiva and daily incidents of dilated pupil were also noted in males and/or females at ≥ 5 mg/kg/day throughout dosing phase. The incidence and severity of these signs were dose-related. All clinical signs resolved immediately after the end of administration, but those observed at 30→25 mg/kg/day were considered to be adverse effects.

 

Coincident with the commencement of dosing, decreases in group mean body weight were noted in males and females at 30→25 mg/kg/day, up to 9.3% and 7.5% on Day 28 respectively, when compared with concurrent controls. Slight body weight loss was also noted in males at 30→25 mg/kg/day and females at ≥ 5 mg/kg/day on Day 7 when compared with the pre-test value on Day -1. The lower group mean body weights correlated with low food consumption. The changes at 30→25 mg/kg/day were not recovered following 14-day recovery period and were considered to be adverse effects.

 

When compared with concurrent controls, slight decreases in food consumption were noted in both sexes at ≥ 5 mg/kg/day on Day 1 and both sexes at 30→25 mg/kg/day throughout the dosing phase (≤ 41% vs controls) and correlated with decreased body weight. The changes in food consumption resolved during recovery phase and were considered to be non-adverse effects due to small in magnitude.

 

When compared with concurrent controls or pre-test value, test article-related decreases in RBC distribution width (RDW, ≤ 5.8% vs controls) and Reticulocyte count (RET, ≤ 43.7% vs controls of absolute and ≤ 41.12% vs controls of percent) were noted in males at ≥ 5 mg/kg/day on Day 29. These changes resolved following 14-day recovery period and were considered to be non-adverse due to small in magnitude and lack histopathology correlates. Test article-related slight but statistical significant increase in Urea (31.70% vs controls) was noted in males at 30→25 mg/kg/day on Day 29. Meanwhile, increases in Urea (≤ 45.68% vs controls) was also noted in both sexes at 30→25 mg/kg/day following 14-day recovery period. These changes were considered to be non-adverse due to small in magnitude and lack histopathology correlates.

 

Oral administration of MEAI resulted in reversible increases in blood pressure (males: ≥5 mg/kg/day, females: ≥15 mg/kg/day) and changes in quantitative ECG parameter (shortening of the PR interval at ≥15 mg/kg/day) and respiratory pattern (tidal volume and respiration rate at ≥5 mg/kg/day) when administered by oral dose to Beagle Dog for up to 28 Days.

 

In conclusion, oral administration of MEAI at doses of 5, 15, or 30→25 mg/kg/day once daily for up to 28 days resulted in mortality at 30→25 mg/kg/day. Therefore, the No-Observed-Adverse-Effect-Level (NOAEL) was considered to be 15 mg/kg/day for both genders, where the Cmax and AUC0-24h on Day 28 were 3690 ng/mL and 33000 h*ng/mL in males, and 5030 ng/mL and 35400 h*ng/mL in females, respectively.

 

Genotoxicity

 

Genotoxicity studies were conducted with MEAI and are summarized below.

 

MEAI: In Vitro Micronucleus Assay in CHO Cells

 

An in vitro GLP study was conducted to evaluate the clastogenic/aneugenic potential of MEAI, in a micronucleus assay using Chinese hamster ovary (CHO-WBL) cells in the absence of activation systems for 3 and 24 hours, and in the presence of activation system (Phenobarbital/5,6-Benzoflavone induced rat liver S9) for 3 hours. All cells were cultured for 24 hours after initiation of test article treatment. The dose range-finding assays were performed to establish the dose range for the definitive micronucleus assay. The definitive micronucleus assay was used to evaluate the clastogenic/aneugenic potential of the test article at concentration of 100, 200 and 400 µg/mL. No significant increases in the percentage of cells with micronuclei were observed at any concentration in the S9-activated 3-hour treatment series and in the non-activated 24-hour treatment series when compared to the concurrent negative control. The frequency of micronucleated cells was comparable with the 99% control limits of the historical negative control data and a concentration-related response was not observed. However, the frequency of micronucleated cells was within the 99% control limits of the historical negative control data, so the significant increases and response were not considered to have biological relevance. Based on the above data, MEAI was concluded to be negative for the induction of micronucleated cells in CHO-WBL cells under the conditions of the current study.

 

87

 

 

MEAI: Bacterial Reverse Mutation Assay

 

An in vitro GLP study was conducted to evaluate the ability of MEAI to induce reverse mutations at the histidine locus of four strains of Salmonella typhimurium (TA98, TA100, TA1535, and TA1537) and at the tryptophan locus of Escherichia coli WP2 uvrA, in the presence and absence of exogenous metabolic activation (β-naphthoflavone (β-NF) and Phenobarbital (PB) induced rat liver S9). A dose range-finding assay was initially conducted using tester strains TA100 and WP2 uvrA in the presence and absence of S9 mix, to establish the dose range for the definitive assay. A definitive mutagenicity assay was then conducted with the strains TA98, TA100, TA1535, TA1537, and WP2 uvrA, in the presence and absence of S9 mix along with the concurrent solvent/negative and positive controls. The dose levels tested with all tester strains ranged between 100 to 5000 µg per plate. No obvious cytotoxicity was observed at any dose level of MEAI with or without S9 mix in any tester strain. No precipitate was observed at any dose level with or without S9 mix in any tester strain. MEAI did not induce more than 2-fold increases in strains TA98, TA100, or WP2 uvrA or 3-fold increases in strains TA1535 or TA1537 in the mean number of revertant colonies at any dose level relative to the concurrent solvent/negative control, in the presence or absence of S9 mix. No dose-response was observed either. It was concluded that MEAI was negative for mutagenicity under the conditions tested.

 

MEAI: Peripheral Blood Micronucleus Assay in Rats

 

An in vivo GLP study was conducted to assess the clastogenic activity of MEAI and if it has and/or disrupts the mitotic apparatus by evaluating its ability to induce an increase of micronuclei frequency in immature erythrocytes of adult Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats after administration by oral gavage. A dose range-finding assay was performed to determine the high dose for the definitive micronucleus assay. The assay consisted of 3 groups of animals (with 3 rats/sex per group), treated once daily by oral gavage for 3 days with vehicle/negative control article (Sterile water for injection) or MEAI (Groups 2 to 3) at 40 or 60 mg/kg/day. Blood samples were collected at 22 (20 to 24) hours post last dosing and examined for the percentage of reticulocytes (RET) among total erythrocytes. After dosing, all animals survived to scheduled termination. Soiled coat and salivation were observed in the 40 and 60 mg/kg/day dose groups. At 60 mg/kg/day, additional signs included hunched posture, abnormal gait, activity decreased, unkempt, nasal discharged, penis extended (males only) and material around mouth/nose (males only). A decrease in body weight gain from Day 4 to Day 1 was noted in the MEAI groups as compared to the controls. When compared with the concurrent control group, reductions in the percentage of reticulocytes (RET) among total erythrocytes were observed at 40 and 60 mg/kg/day dose groups. The respective decreases were 34.83% and 51.24% for males, and 45.76% and 35.59% for females. Based on the above results and considering that there were no obvious differences in toxicity findings between male and female rats, 40 mg/kg/day was selected as the high dose and only male rats were used in the definitive assay. In the definitive micronucleus assay, 27 rats were assigned to 5 groups with 5 animals per group (7 animals for the high dose group) and treated with vehicle/negative control article (Group 1), MEAI (Groups 2 to 4) or positive control (Group 5). The dose levels in Groups 2, 3 and 4 were 10, 20 and 40 mg/kg/day. Vehicle/Negative control article and MEAI were administered once daily by oral gavage for 3 days to animals at the dose volume of 10 mL/kg. The positive control (Cyclophosphamide monohydrate) was given to rats once daily at 6 mg/kg/day for 3 consecutive days by oral gavage at a dose volume of 10 mL/kg. At 22 (20 to 24) hours post last dosing, blood samples were collected from each animal for micronucleus frequency analysis. After dosing, all animals survived to scheduled termination. Abnormal gait was found in all test article dose groups, scab (mouth) was found in one rat of the 40 mg/kg/day dose group, and ocular discharge was found in one rat in the 10 mg/kg/day dose group. No abnormal clinical signs were found in any other groups. On Day 4, compared with Day 1, a dose-related decrease in body weight gain was noted at 20 and 40 mg/kg/day as compared to the controls. Reductions (29.79%) in the percentage of reticulocytes (RET) among total erythrocytes were observed in the 40 mg/kg/day dose group, when compared with the concurrent control group. No statistically significant increases in micronucleus formation (p>0.05) were observed in any MEAI dose groups when compared with control article group. No significant dose-related increase response in micronucleus frequency was identified by statistical analysis for test article treatment groups (Cochran-Armitage, p>0.05). The micronucleus frequencies of all test article dose groups were within the 99% control limits of the historical negative control data range. Based on these results, MEAI was considered negative in this rat peripheral blood micronucleus assay.

 

Special Toxicity Studies

 

The potential neurotoxicity of MEAI was examined in an acute neurotoxicity GLP study in rats. This study was conducted in accordance with the ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline M3 (R2). Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human Clinical Trials and Marketing Authorization for Pharmaceuticals. 200 fasted Sprague Dawley rats (100/ sex) were randomly assigned to 5 groups of 20/sex each and were administered either with a predetermined single dose of MEAI (low dose 20 mg/kg, mid dose of 40 mg/kg and high dose of 80 mg/kg) by oral gavage or vehicle (sterile water) by oral gavage or MK-801 (5 mg/kg via IP injection), an NMDA antagonist known to be neurotoxic. Animals were monitored for viability, clinical observations, body weights, food consumption. After dosing, the first 10 rats/sex/group from all groups were necropsied on Day 3 (after 48 hours post-dose). The last 10 rats/sex/group from all groups were allocated for an additional 13-day observation period and were necropsied on Day 14. At necropsy, animals were evaluated for gross pathology, organ weights and histopathology.

 

88

 

 

After the completion of dosing on Day 1, 11 treated animals at 40 mg/kg MEAI (1 male and 1 female) and 80 mg/kg MEAI (2 males and 7 females) were found dead. Prior to being found dead, clinical signs including slight to severe salivation, decreased activity, tremors, piloerection, atonia, unkempt, skin discolored (ears, forefeet and hindfeet, red), ataxia and prostration were noted. Macroscopic observations including multifocal red discoloration in thymus of one male at 40 mg/kg, multifocal to coalescing/diffuse dark discoloration in lungs of two females and bilateral multifocal pale discoloration in eyes of one female at 80 mg/kg were noted. There were no MEAI related changes in body weight and food consumption. Test article related clinical signs were noted at ≥ 20 mg/kg MEAI, and included hunched posture prostration, salivation, tremors, decreased activity, ataxia, atonia, piloerection, skin discolored and unkempt. All above clinical signs except piloerection, ataxia and thin were noted in animals administered with MK-801 at 5 mg/kg.

 

Test article-related finding was scattered to individual neuronal necrosis in the regions of the motor, somatosensory, entorhinal, visual, and piriform cortices, as well as within the thalamus, hypothalamus, basal nuclei/striatum, and medulla oblongata.

 

In conclusion, MEAI when administered once via oral gavage to fasted rats at 20, 40 or 80 mg/kg followed by a 13-day observation period resulted in test article-related mortality at ≥ 40 mg/kg. Test article related clinical signs were noted in all treated groups. Test article-related microscopic changes were noted at ≥ 20 mg/kg. Therefore, under the conditions of the study, the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was considered to be 20 mg/kg.

 

Bar-Ilan University Study: Testing 2-FDCK as an Alternative Treatment for Major Depression Disorder

 

An exploratory efficacy study utilizing the Flinders Sensitive Line (FSL) rat model for depression was conducted to determine 2-Fluorodeschloroketamine’s (2-FDCK's) effect on depressive-like behavior in comparison to Ketamine. 2FDCK or Ketamine (10mg/kg/day IP) was given to FSL rats for 14 consecutive days. Motivational state measurements (forced swim test, or FST) were conducted 1 hour, 7 days and 14 days post final treatment day to assess potential acute as well as long-term effects. In addition, both male (n=10 per group) and female (n=4 per group) rats were included in the study to investigate possible gender differences. The results were mixed with some animals showing a reduction in depressive-like behavior and some showing no effect. It was decided to use a K-cluster test to evaluate the data; this test is a method that enables separation of two different sub-groups with statistical significance in a non-biased manner with high integrity. As expected, among the responders, Ketamine acutely alleviated depressive-like behavior in male FSL rats as measured by the 1-hour FST but did not reach significance at the 7 and 14 days timepoints (comparison within the group to baseline measurement). Conversely, the 2FDCK male responders reached significant improvements in all three timepoints checked compared to baseline measurement (1 hour, 7 days, 14 days), suggesting a long-term effect on top of the acute one for 2FDCK. When comparing specifically the long-term effect (14-day FST) between the whole male groups (Ketamine vs 2FDCK), a significant effect was found in favor of 2FDCK. Females were later assessed in smaller groups due to technical limitations of the study. Despite the small number of animals, Ketamine treated females showed a reduction in depressive-like behavior during the 7-day FST but not during the 1-hour and 14-day assessments. Conversely, 2FDCK treated females showed significant improvements in the 1-hour and 14-day assessments but not in the 7-day timepoint. In order to rule out the possibility that the effects observed were due to physical motoric side effects and not due to the anti-depressive properties of the substances, an open field test was conducted where rats were allowed to explore an arena for 10 minutes and their locomotion and velocity was monitored. Ketamine treated animals showed a significant reduction in velocity after treatment as compared to before treatment, as opposed to the 2FDCK group where no significant effect was observed. These results suggest that there is a significant difference between the effect of Ketamine on physical performance and no such effect for 2FDCK.

 

In conclusion, these results suggest that there is a long-term effect for 2-FDCK vs Ketamine on the depressive-like behavior of the FSL male rodent model. As described above, both Ketamine and 2-FDCK affected depressive-like symptoms, however, this effect was maintained for a long-term when using the chronic treatment paradigm, only for 2-FDCK. Female FSL rats mimic the same phenomena in response to 2-FDCK despite the small number of animals assessed.

 

Competition

 

The pharmaceutical industry is intensely competitive and subject to rapid and significant technological change. Our potential competitors include large and experienced companies that have significant competitive advantages over us, such as greater financial, research and development, manufacturing, personnel and marketing resources, greater brand recognition, and more experience and expertise in obtaining marketing approvals from the FDA and foreign regulatory authorities. These companies may develop new drugs to treat the indications that we target or seek to have existing drugs approved for use in the indications that we target.

 

These potential competitors may therefore introduce competing products without our prior knowledge and without our ability to take preemptive measures in anticipation of their commercial launch. Competition may increase further as a result of advances in the commercial applicability of technologies and greater availability of capital for investment in this industry. Our competitors may succeed in developing, acquiring or licensing on an exclusive basis, products that are more effective, easier to administer or less costly than our product candidates.is highly competitive, with new approaches and technologies regularly emerging. We expect to face competition across our current programs and with any future programs we may seek to develop and/or commercialize from major pharmaceutical, biotechnology, specialty pharmaceutical and generic pharmaceutical companies among others. Potential competitors also include academic institutions, governmental agencies and other public and private research organizations that conduct research, seek patent protection and establish collaborative arrangements for research, development, manufacturing and commercialization.

 

89
